mainTopic: Joining another's נזירות with 'וַאֲנִי': the time limit, and whether each joiner attaches to the one before him or to the first
overview: The גמרא brings a ברייתא showing that 'וַאֲנִי' (And I) only joins a friend's נזירות vow if it is said within כדי דיבור, the time a student takes to greet his רב. It tries to prove from the משנה's two 'וַאֲנִי's that no more can join. That proof is pushed off: a תנא is not a peddler who lists endlessly, and two were needed only to create a middle person for the משנה's later clause. Then an איבעיא is raised: does each person attach to the one right before him, or does everyone attach to the first? The difference is whether the chain can go on forever. Proofs from the משנה's clauses about releasing the first or the last person are each pushed off. Finally, a ברייתא says openly that releasing the middle person releases everyone after him, so each person attaches to the one before him. The amud ends by starting the next case of the משנה: how can saying 'my mouth is like his mouth and my hair is like his hair' make someone a נזיר?

steps.title: A ברייתא confirms the time limit for saying 'And I'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if the friend waited longer than כדי דיבור before saying 'וַאֲנִי', only the first person is a נזיר. It also defines כדי דיבור as the time a student takes to greet his רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way in a ברייתא: Someone said 'I am hereby a נזיר.' His friend heard, waited the length of כדי דיבור, and then said 'And I.' The first person is bound, and the friend is free. How long is כדי דיבור? The time it takes a student to greet his teacher.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports what was just said: 'וַאֲנִי' only works if it is said right away, within כדי דיבור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא shows the flip side of the rule. If the friend waits a full כדי דיבור, his 'וַאֲנִי' is too late and does not attach to the vow. It also gives a measure for כדי דיבור: the few words of a student greeting his רב.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way (a ברייתא that supports the previous statement)
The short time it takes to say a brief phrase
'And I': words a person says to join someone else's vow
A greeting, asking after someone's welfare

steps.whyThisMatters: The measure of כדי דיבור, a student greeting his רב, is used in many places in הלכה for how quickly one statement must follow another to count as connected.

phrases.english: It was also taught this way:
One who said, 'I am hereby a nazirite,'
and his friend heard and waited the time of speaking a phrase,
and then said, 'And I'
he is bound, and his friend is permitted.
And how long is the time of speaking?
The time it takes a student to greet his teacher.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the statement made just before this section, that 'וַאֲנִי' must be said within כדי דיבור.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that 'וַאֲנִי' only works within כדי דיבור
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא ruling that after waiting a full כדי דיבור the friend is not a נזיר

steps.title: Trying to prove from the משנה that only two can join
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the משנה's listing of 'וַאֲנִי' only twice shows that no more people can join, because too much time has passed since the first vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say the משנה supports this? It says: Someone said 'I am hereby a נזיר,' his friend heard and said 'And I,' and another said 'And I.' Only twice, and no more!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to find support in the משנה, pointing out that it lists 'וַאֲנִי' only two times.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that the משנה stopped at two on purpose. A third 'וַאֲנִי' would come more than כדי דיבור after the first vow, so it would no longer count. This assumes that everyone is measured against the first person's vow.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say this supports him? (a proposed proof)

phrases.english: Shall we say this supports him?
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the view that the time limit of כדי דיבור counts, as stated just before.

phrases.english: One who said, 'I am hereby a nazirite,'
and his friend heard and said 'And I,' 'And I,'
phrases.notes: Two different people each said 'And I,' one after the other.

phrases.english: and no more!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ברייתא, the גמרא looks for further support in the משנה itself.
steps.raayaObject: That only a limited number can join, because of the כדי דיבור limit from the first vow

steps.title: The תנא is not a peddler listing endlessly
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected: the תנא had to stop somewhere and was not going to repeat 'וַאֲנִי' over and over like a peddler calling out his goods.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should the תנא keep counting like a peddler and go on and on?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from the previous step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Stopping at two does not show that a third person cannot join. A משנה does not list every possible number of people. It gives an example and stops.

keyTerms.meaning: The teacher of the משנה or ברייתא
A peddler, who calls out his wares one after another

phrases.english: Should the teacher, like a peddler,
keep counting and going on?!
phrases.notes: A peddler reels off his items one after another. The משנה doesn't do that; it gives a short example.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof suggested in step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the inference from the number of times 'וַאֲנִי' appears
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A משנה naturally stops listing at some point, so stopping at two proves nothing about a limit

steps.title: Then why not list just one 'And I'?
steps.stepSummary: If the תנא did not want to list endlessly, he should have given only one 'וַאֲנִי' and let us learn the rest from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then let him teach just one, and teach us these others from it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rejection: if the goal was to be short, one 'וַאֲנִי' would have been enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rejection in step 3 explained why the תנא did not list many. But it does not explain why he listed two instead of one. Listing exactly two still looks like it means something.

phrases.english: But let him teach one,
and teach us these others from it!
phrases.notes: 'These' means all the other people who say 'And I.' We could learn them from one example.

steps.kashyaTarget: The rejection that the תנא just stopped listing
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If brevity was the reason, the תנא should have listed only one 'וַאֲנִי'. Listing two seems deliberate.

steps.title: Two are listed because the later clause needs a middle person
steps.stepSummary: True, one would be enough. But the משנה's later clause speaks of 'the first' and 'the last' and implies someone in the middle, so the תנא needed three people: the vower plus two who said 'וַאֲנִי'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Indeed so. But because the later clause teaches: if the first was released, they are all released; if the last was released, the last is released and all the others stay bound, this shows there is a middle person. That is why it says 'And I, and I.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by pointing to the end of the משנה, which needs a first, a middle, and a last person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סיפא contrasts 'the first' with 'the last' and says 'all the others' stay bound. That only makes sense if there is at least one person in between. So two 'וַאֲנִי's are there to set up three people, not to cap the number who may join.

keyTerms.meaning: The later clause of the משנה
Was released from his vow by a חכם

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's two 'וַאֲנִי's do not prove a limit of two joiners. They exist only to create a 'middle' person for the סיפא about releasing the first or the last.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the משנה limits joining to two people. The גמרא just explained that the number two comes from the needs of the סיפא, not from a rule.

phrases.english: Indeed, that is so,
but because it teaches in the later clause:
if the first was released, they are all released;
if the last was released
the last is permitted and all the others are bound;
this implies that there is a middle person,
and that is why it teaches 'And I,' 'And I.'

steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the wording of the רישא by the needs of the סיפא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Listing 'וַאֲנִי' twice seemed to mean that only two may join
steps.terutzMaskana: Two are listed only to create a middle person for the סיפא's case of first and last

steps.title: Does each person attach to the one before him or to the first?
steps.stepSummary: An איבעיא: when several people say 'וַאֲנִי' in a row, does each attach to the person just before him, or do all attach to the first person's vow?
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: Does each one attach to his friend before him, or perhaps they all attach to the first?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about how a chain of 'וַאֲנִי' works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to see the chain. Either each joiner hooks onto the person who spoke just before him, or every joiner hooks directly onto the first person's original vow.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked before them (the חכמים)

phrases.english: A question was asked:
Does each one attach to his friend,
phrases.notes: 'His friend' means the person who spoke right before him in the chain.

phrases.english: or perhaps they all attach to the first?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the same topic of several people joining, now asking how the chain works.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether each joiner attaches to the person before him or to the first vower

steps.title: What practical difference does it make?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what difference there is between the two sides of the question.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the practical result of the question, setting up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before trying to answer an איבעיא, the גמרא often clarifies what changes in practice. This line prepares for that explanation.

phrases.english: What practical difference is there?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical result of the איבעיא in step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical outcome that depends on the איבעיא

steps.title: The difference: can the chain go on forever?
steps.stepSummary: If each attaches to the one before him, people can keep joining endlessly. If all attach to the first, no one can join once more than כדי דיבור has passed since the first vow. The גמרא then asks which side is right. Steps 17-18 settle it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference is whether they can keep attaching on and on. If you say each attaches to his friend, they can keep attaching forever. If you say they attach to the first, they cannot attach after more than כדי דיבור. So what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the practical difference and then restates the question, asking which side is right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If each person hooks onto the one just before him, every new joiner only needs to speak within כדי דיבור of the last speaker, so the chain never has to end. If everyone hooks onto the first person, the clock runs from the first vow, and once כדי דיבור has passed no one else can join. The גמרא ends with 'מאי?', and the next steps try to answer it.

keyTerms.meaning: To keep attaching on and on

steps.whyThisMatters: This connects back to the earlier proof: limiting joiners would only make sense if everyone attaches to the first person.

phrases.english: Whether they can keep attaching on and on.
If you say each one attaches to his friend,
they can keep attaching forever.
phrases.notes: As long as each new person speaks right after the one before him.

phrases.english: And if you say they attach to the first,
they cannot attach after more than the time of speaking.
phrases.notes: The time is counted from the first person's vow.

phrases.english: What is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'what difference' question of step 7 and restates the איבעיא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The difference is whether the chain is unlimited (each attaches to the previous person) or ends after כדי דיבור from the first vow (all attach to the first).

steps.title: A proof from the משנה listing only two people who said 'And I'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues that since the משנה stops after two 'וַאֲנִי's, everyone must attach to the first person's vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: the משנה says one person said 'I am a נזיר', another heard and said 'And I', and another said 'And I', and nothing more. This shows they all attach to the first one. If each attached to the one right before him, the משנה should have listed many 'And I's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a proof from the משנה to answer the question of Step 6. It argues that all attach to the first person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If each person attached to the one just before him, the chain could go on forever, so the משנה should have shown a long chain. Since the משנה stops after only two, it seems that the chain is limited. A limited chain fits the view that everyone hangs on the first vow, within כדי דיבור of it.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it: draws a conclusion from a source
They attach (their vow onto another's vow)
It would enter your mind: introduces an assumption the גמרא is testing

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"I am hereby a nazir," and his fellow heard
and said "And I," "And I,"
phrases.notes: This is quoting our משנה: one person says 'And I,' then a third person says 'And I.'

phrases.english: and nothing more,
learn from it that it is onto the first that they attach,
for if it would enter your mind
that each one attaches to his fellow,
let it teach many "And I"s!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins trying to answer the open איבעיא from Steps 6-8 by using the wording of the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That all who say 'וַאֲנִי' attach to the first person's vow.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה lists only two 'וַאֲנִי's and no more.

steps.title: The תנא does not list endlessly like a peddler
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed off: the תנא simply had no reason to keep listing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should the תנא keep counting on and on like a peddler?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof. Stopping at two does not mean the chain stops at two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A peddler calls out every item he sells, one after another, but a תנא does not teach that way. Stopping after two 'וַאֲנִי's is just a way of teaching briefly. It tells us nothing about whether a longer chain works.

keyTerms.meaning: A peddler, who calls out all his wares one by one

phrases.english: Should the tanna, like a peddler,
phrases.notes: A peddler calls out every item he has for sale. A תנא doesn't need to list every case like that.

phrases.english: keep counting on and on?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of Step 9, using the same reasoning the גמרא used earlier in the sugya.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole proof from the number of 'וַאֲנִי's.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumes the תנא would list every possible case. A תנא teaches briefly and does not list endlessly.

steps.title: Then the משנה should have listed only one 'And I'
steps.stepSummary: If the תנא wanted to be brief, one 'וַאֲנִי' would have been enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then let him teach just one, and we would learn all of them from it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rejection. If being brief is the reason, why did the תנא give two 'וַאֲנִי's and not one?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rejection in Step 10 said the תנא kept it short. But the shortest way would be a single 'וַאֲנִי'. So the second 'וַאֲנִי' still needs a reason. This repeats the challenge from Step 4, now raised inside the proof attempt.

keyTerms.meaning: And let us learn all of them from it

phrases.english: But let him teach one
and let us learn all of them from it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection in Step 10. The גמרא is repeating the Step 4 challenge, with almost the same words (כולהון instead of הני), in this new setting.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 10 that the תנא was only being brief.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being brief would mean one 'וַאֲנִי', not two, so the second one still needs a reason.

steps.title: Two 'And I's were needed to have a middle person
steps.stepSummary: The משנה's later clause about 'the first' and 'the last' implies a middle person, so the תנא needed three people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the משנה teaches 'if the first was released, they are all released; if the last was released, the last is permitted and all the others are bound,' it implies there is a middle one. That is why it teaches 'And I,' 'And I.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The second 'וַאֲנִי' is there to create a middle person, not to show that the chain stops at two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'the last' and 'all the others are bound' only make sense if there are at least three people. So the תנא needed two 'וַאֲנִי's to fit his later wording. This restores the rejection, and the proof from Step 9 falls.

keyTerms.meaning: Since it teaches: the wording is explained by another clause
Was released (his vow was undone by a חכם)

phrases.english: Since it teaches
"If the first was released, they are all released,"
"If the last was released,
the last is permitted and all the others are bound,"
by implication there is a middle one,
therefore it teaches "And I," "And I."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 11 with the same answer as Step 5, which closes off the first proof attempt.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the wording through another clause of the same משנה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two 'וַאֲנִי's means the chain stops at two, or at least that one would have been enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two 'וַאֲנִי's were needed only to have a first, a middle, and a last person, so no proof can be drawn from the number.

steps.title: A proof from 'if the first was released, all are released'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues that because the משנה mentions only the first person's release, releasing the middle person would not release the later ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'If the first was released, they are all released.' Only when the first is released are they all released, but not when the middle one is released. Learn from this that they all attach to the first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second proof from the משנה. This time it uses the clause about undoing the vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If each person attached to the one before him, then releasing the middle person should also release everyone after him. The משנה picks the first person, which suggests that only his release brings the others down. That suggests everyone depends directly on the first.

keyTerms.meaning: But this one, no: draws an inference from what the text leaves out

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"If the first was released, they are all released."
It is the first whom they released,
but the middle one, no,
learn from it that they attach onto the first.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הוּתַּר הָרִאשׁוֹן — הוּתְּרוּ כּוּלָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof failed, the גמרא tries a new proof from a different clause of the same משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That all who say 'וַאֲנִי' attach to the first person's vow.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's clause 'if the first was released, they are all released', read as excluding the middle person.

steps.title: The משנה chose the first person only to say 'all are released'
steps.stepSummary: Each may still attach to the one before him. The תנא picked the first only because releasing him releases everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: I can tell you: really, each attaches to the one before him. But the תנא wanted to say 'they are ALL released.' If he had taught the middle one, there would still be the first, who is not released. That is why he taught the first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the second proof. The choice of the first person tells us nothing about who attaches to whom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if each person hangs on the one before him, releasing the middle person would free only those after him, not the first. To be able to say 'all of them are released,' the תנא had to pick the first person. So the wording fits both sides, and the next steps keep looking for an answer.

keyTerms.meaning: I can say to you: introduces a different way to read the source
Really, actually: keeps the original position

steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs so far from the משנה fail. The number of 'וַאֲנִי's and the choice of the first person are both explained by how the תנא worded things, so these proofs do not settle the איבעיא. One more proof from the משנה comes in step 15, and a ברייתא in step 17 settles it.

phrases.english: I can say to you:
really, each one attaches to his fellow.
But since it wanted to teach "they are all released,"
for if it had taught the middle one,
there would be the first, who is not released,
therefore it teaches the first.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימָא לָךְ: לְעוֹלָם חַד בְּחַבְרֵיהּ מִתְּפִיס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the second proof in Step 13.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the inference that releasing the middle person would not release those after him.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The תנא chose the first person so he could say 'all are released.' That is about wording, not about who attaches to whom.

steps.title: Proof from the משנה's wording about the last person
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says that if the last person is released, only he is released. That implies that releasing the middle person would also release the person after him, so each one attaches to the one before him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if the last one was released, the last is released and all the others stay bound. That is because nobody comes after him. But if the middle one was released, there is someone after him, and that person is released too. Learn from this: each one attaches to his friend.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a new proof from the משנה. It reads the rule about 'the last person' carefully to learn how the vows connect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives a reason-like detail: only the last one is released. The גמרא reads that as hinting that he stands alone only because nobody follows him. So a middle person who is released would bring down the one after him, which means each person hangs on the one right before him.

keyTerms.meaning: was released (his vow was cancelled by a חכם)
each one attaches himself to his friend (the one right before him)

phrases.english: Come and hear: if the last one was released —
the last one is released and all the others are bound.
That is because there is no one else after him,
but the middle one,
who has someone else after him — that one is released too.
Learn from this: each one attaches to his friend.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from 'the first' was pushed off in step 14, the גמרא tries a proof from the משנה's clause about 'the last.'
steps.raayaObject: That each later person attaches to the one right before him
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's clause: 'If the last was released, the last is released and all are bound'

steps.title: 'Last' really means the middle one
steps.stepSummary: Maybe everyone attaches to the first person. The משנה's word 'last' really means the middle one, and it was called 'last' only to match the word 'first.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, I can tell you that they all attach to the first one. And what does 'last' in the משנה mean? The middle one. Since the תנא said 'first,' he also said 'last.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes off the proof. It says the משנה's word 'last' is not exact.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If everyone attaches only to the first person, then releasing anyone except the first releases only himself. Read this way, 'the last' means any person after the first, including the middle one. The תנא used the word 'last' just to pair nicely with 'first,' so nothing can be learned from that word.

keyTerms.meaning: really, I can tell you (the start of a pushback)
since (he used one word, he used the matching word too)

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'אַחֲרוֹן' (last) is being read as 'אֶמְצָעִי' (middle). The word is not taken literally. It was chosen only to pair with 'רִאשׁוֹן' (first).

phrases.english: Really, I can tell you:
they all attach to the first one,
and what is the 'last' that it teaches? The middle one,
and since he taught 'first,' he taught 'last.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 15 by reading 'last' loosely.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the inference from the word 'last' entirely
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed 'last' was meant exactly. It may just be a word chosen to match 'first' and really mean the middle one.

steps.title: A ברייתא says it openly: release the middle and everyone after is released
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא openly says that if the middle person is released, everyone after him is released and everyone before him stays bound. This proves each one attaches to the one before him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, as a ברייתא teaches openly: if the first was released, all are released. If the last was released, the last is released and all the others are bound. If the middle was released, he and everyone after him are released, and everyone before him stays bound. Learn from this: each one attaches to his friend.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that spells out the middle case directly, so it cannot be pushed off.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה left the middle case unclear, which allowed the pushbacks. The ברייתא states plainly that releasing the middle one releases those after him. That only makes sense if each person's vow hangs on the one right before him.

phrases.english: Come and hear, as it is taught openly:
if the first was released, they are all released;

phrases.aramaic: הוּתַּר הָאַחֲרוֹן — הָאַחֲרוֹן מוּתָּר וְכוּלָּן אֲסוּרִין,
phrases.english: if the last was released, the last is released and all the others are bound;
if the middle one was released, from him and after him are released,
phrases.notes: Literally 'downward,' meaning the people who spoke after him in the chain.

steps.title: Conclusion: each attaches to the one before him
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the proof from the ברייתא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the discussion by accepting that each person attaches to the one right before him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ends the back-and-forth that ran through the earlier steps. The ברייתא's clear words decide the question that the משנה left open.

keyTerms.meaning: learn from this (said here as final agreement)

steps.whatToRemember: When several people say 'and I' one after another, each one hangs his נזירות on the person right before him. Release the first and everyone is released. Release the middle one and he and everyone after him are released. Release the last and only he is released.

phrases.english: Learn from this.

steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: חד בחבריה מתפיס: each person attaches to the one right before him.

steps.title: How do 'mouth' and 'hair' words make someone a נזיר?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the next case in the משנה. Someone says 'my mouth is like his mouth and my hair is like his hair' after hearing a friend vow נזירות, and the גמרא asks why that should make him a נזיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: one said 'I am a נזיר,' and his friend heard and said 'my mouth is like his mouth and my hair is like his hair,' and so on. Just because he said 'my mouth is like his mouth and my hair is like his hair,' is he a נזיר?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new section by quoting the משנה. It then challenges the משנה's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second person never said the word נזיר. He only compared his mouth and hair to his friend's. The גמרא asks how such vague words can make him a נזיר, and this sets up the answer in the next step.

my hair is like his hair
